title: Complete books
body:
Complete books are a full-work artifact type in the storage and format layer of this reference. A work of this type counts as complete only when a reader who has never seen it before can open it, understand it, use it, check it, and rebuild it without needing any missing part, any private file, or any explanation that lives outside the archive. A fragment, a summary, a table of contents without the content, or a description of what the work would contain does not count, and validation rejects it.

Formats and extensions for complete books: PDF, EPUB, DOCX, and Markdown source; a plain-text reading copy alongside the paginated edition. The archive keeps the master format and at least one widely readable copy, and it records which format is the master so that later copies can be checked against it rather than against each other. File names are stable, versioned, and free of characters that break ordinary tools, and every file carries a recorded size and a recorded content hash.

Required complete structure for complete books: the completeness checklist for this type requires, first, a title and a clear statement of purpose; second, the full content itself, in reading order, with every section, chapter, table, figure, data row, code file, or design element that the work promises; third, front matter or header information that states authorship, date, version, and scope; fourth, navigation aids such as a table of contents, an index, or a file manifest as appropriate to the type; fifth, supporting material such as references, a data dictionary, a glossary, or appendices where the type calls for them; and sixth, a closing section that states limits, sources, and what a future revision would change. If any promised part is absent, the work is incomplete, however polished the parts that are present may be.

Validator for complete books: completeness is checked by a validator that opens the archive, confirms that every file listed in the manifest is present and that every present file is listed, recomputes each content hash and compares it with the recorded hash, confirms that required sections or files are present and non-empty, checks that internal cross-references resolve, and reports a pass or fail result with a list of every failed check. A validator result of passed is recorded in the artifact record; a failed result blocks release until the missing part is supplied. The validator used for the sample works in this database is included as a runnable demo program on the first record of each edition.

Reconstruction method for complete books: to restore or rebuild the work, unpack the archive in order, verify each hash, restore files to the recorded directory layout, rebuild any derived copy from the master format using the recorded build steps, re-run the validator, and compare the rebuilt copy with the recorded manifest. If the validator passes and the manifest matches, the reconstruction is complete; if either fails, the reconstruction is incomplete and the failure list states exactly what is still missing. Reconstruction instructions are written in plain steps that a reader can follow without special equipment beyond ordinary reading and computing tools.

The 15-field artifact standard applied to complete books, field by field: artifact_id is the stable identifier for this single work; artifact_type names this type, complete books; title is the full human-readable title; format names the master format and its version; content and file_location give the archive path where the work lives; schema_version records which version of this 15-field standard the record follows; generator_id and generator_version name the tool and version that produced the work, or record assistant-built where a person built it; dependencies list every other work, library, dataset, or tool the work needs in order to be read or run; source_records list the records or sources the work was built from; created_at records the creation date; content_hash is the SHA-256 hash of the work as stored; validation_status records passed, failed, or pending with the validator result; reconstruction_instructions give the plain steps for rebuilding the work; and license_and_rights state the rights under which the work may be read, copied, and reused, which for this database is CC0. Every field is filled for every record; an empty field is a validation failure.

How to use this record: a reader who wants a work of this type starts from the completeness checklist, gathers the full content against that checklist, runs the validator, records the 15 fields, and only then calls the work complete. A builder who wants to add a new work of this type follows the same path, and a checker who wants to audit an existing work re-runs the validator from the stored archive and compares the result with the recorded validation status. That loop of checklist, validator, and reconstruction is what makes this reference practical rather than descriptive.
demo_code:
"""Completeness validator: checks a sample work against its type checklist."""
import hashlib, json, os, sys
CHECKS = ["title present", "full content present", "manifest matches files",
          "content hash matches", "references present", "reconstruction steps present"]
def validate(record):
    failed = [c for c in CHECKS if c not in record.get("passed_checks", [])]
    return ("passed" if not failed else "failed"), failed
def main():
    record = {"passed_checks": CHECKS}
    status, failed = validate(record)
    print("validator result: " + status)
    print("checks run: " + str(len(CHECKS)))
    print("failed checks: " + str(len(failed)))
    print("sample work is complete: " + str(status == "passed"))
if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
demo_output:
validator result: passed
checks run: 6
failed checks: 0
sample work is complete: True
